The layouts are nearly identical; Chad normally uses a darker blue stripe than Romania.
Both are red over white; their official proportions differ, so trivia choices keep the original ratios.
Both use green, white, and orange vertical bands, but the order is reversed.
Both use horizontal red, white, and blue; Luxembourg normally uses a lighter blue and a longer proportion.
Australia includes the Commonwealth Star and more stars; New Zealand's four Southern Cross stars are red-edged in white.
Qatar is maroon with nine white serration points; Bahrain is red with five.
All use yellow, blue, and red; Ecuador adds its coat of arms and Venezuela adds an arc of stars.
Both use the same three colours in vertical bands, but in opposite order.
Both use green, white, and red vertical bands; Mexico places its national coat of arms in the centre.
Both use black, red, and yellow; Belgium's bands are vertical and Germany's are horizontal.
Both use an offset Nordic cross; Norway is red with a blue inner cross, while Iceland reverses those dominant colours.
Both use a white Nordic cross on red, but Norway adds a blue cross inside the white one.
All use white, blue, and red horizontal bands; Slovenia and Slovakia add different national arms, while Russia does not.
All use red, white, and blue horizontal bands; Croatia and Paraguay add national emblems, while the Netherlands does not.
All are blue-white-blue; Honduras has five stars, while Nicaragua and El Salvador use different central arms.
These flags share red, white, and black bands; their central stars, text, emblems, or lack of them distinguish the designs.
These flags reuse green, yellow, and red vertical bands; order and central stars are the quickest clues.
These flags share Pan-Arab colours; compare the hoist shape and the order of the horizontal bands.
Both have five horizontal red, white, and blue bands; the broad centre band is red for Costa Rica and blue for Thailand.
Both are simple white-and-red bicolours; Poland is white over red and Indonesia is red over white.
